Title: First Strike - what to do with it

Messages.Author: prea...@utanet.at
Messages.Body:
In the light of a possible reworking of the rules (for the
pre-constructed starters or perhaps Sabbat-starters) I would like to
talk a bit about the First Strike rule.

Please note that I don't take RPG-related stuff into account in this
post, as I think that we should concentrate purely on the mechanics
here.

The current situation:
First Strike resolves *after* S:CE and dodge. Period.

This essentially means FS is a rather useless concept, as it gets beaten
by the two most common anti-combat strategies: S:CE and dodge.
There is only a limited number of FS cards available, and some of them
are very limited (stealing/destroying equipment or hand/melee strikes
only or only blocking vampire).
Here is the list:
- Equipment based
Shattering Blow (pot)
Fast Hands (cel)
Blessing of Durga Syn (chi)
Canine Horde (ani)
- hand/melee strikes only
Silence of Death (qui)
- blocking vamp only
Backstab (cel)

The equipment based cards see infrequently use, whereas the others are
underused par excellence.
I've *never* seen anyone using Backstab. I considered it using myself
once, but discarded the idea due to high blood cost (2) and the
inability to hurt anti-combat decks (S:CE and dodge). Too much resources
for almost nothing. I consider Backstab a wallpaper card. (You gain also
an additional for CEL, but why would you bother with an additional
strike if you intend to kill with FS??? It's quite redundant.)
Silence of Death is also quite useless, Assamites are seldom played at
the moment, and even if you see a deck with them, they don't have
Silences in it.

Quite another thing is the often-feared Muddled Vampire Hunter. With 4
hand damage, FS, built-in rush ablilty, he is the bane of many weenies.
However, as he is an ally, he is also not very often seen in play.
Granted, there are some ally-madness decks, but they tend not to be
effective, VP-wise.

What do we have:
We have a concept that is rather underused (lets put it that way), but
the point is, it *is* in the rule-book, which means just another thing
newbies will learn and have to take into account.
IMO, and in many others, this is an undesireable situation.

There are 3 solutions for it:

1.) Skip the FS concept alltogether in the new rule-book. (Just like it
was done with paralyze) I believe it would be possible to mimic the
effect on the respective card with special text (a la wooden stake).
This would slim down the rule-book and the rules are a *bit* streamlined
so it would be easier for newbies to learn.

2.) Make FS beat dodge and S:CE. Or put in other words: make dodge and
S:CE resolve *after* strikes dealt with FS. This would be quite
reasonable for newbies ("FS resolves before all other strikes without
FS") and also would provide a new way to beat S:CE and dodge.

3.) Make FS beat dodge (not S:CE). This would make one exception in the
rules ("dodge negates the opponent's strike, even if it was dealt with
FS") obsolete, makes FS stronger, and keeps the S:CE the "combat
suppressor" like it is now (and should be to *some* extent).

I personally like solution 3 best, as it enhances FS, but doesn't make
it overpowering at the same time. It would make the rules a little
easier (for newbies at least), as FS really happens before the other
strike then (S:CE would still be the exception, but that's ok, cause it
stands for the power to prohibit combat altogether in the RPG (which
should not be an argument, yes I know)) and so would be more intuitive
than it is now (at least for newbies).
To battle S:CE with FS would not be ideal IMO, I think that could better
be solved with individual cards.

Well, the FS-concept would be useless, even if it beat dodge, if no new
cards would take advantage of it. (How much equipment will
combat-avoidance decks have anyway?)
The Assamites could have a Contract-based card that exploits FS in some
fashion, also a slightly less useful cel-based FS card might also be
cool; however, this card could be given to aus instead.

To beat S:CE I would suggest a qui-card and an aus card (so Tremere and
Tzimisce can participate in the anti-S:CE party, too).

Well, I've posted my opinions on FS. I really think it's better to kill
the concept rather than let it live on the current way. Better would be
a re-write though.

Carl

>FS") obsolete, makes FS stronger, and keeps the S:CE the "combat
>suppressor" like it is now (and should be to *some* extent).

I don't care for any of these. There's no reason in the world to completely
discard First Strike. And you screw up whatever card balance you have by
tinkering with a major rule like this.

Nor are these the only option. I like solution 4 best: create cards that
make First Strike useful as it.

Benificial creature enchantments in Magic have this problem. The original
Magic game and several years of expansions flew in the face of the card
disadvantage problem that beneficial creature enchantments posed to
deckbuilders. Hence, in tournament play, with a few specific exceptions,
players ignored beneficial creature enchantment cards in droves. Finally,
after years of seeing this, the Magic designers *finally* started to use
some imagination and figured out beneficial creature enchantments that either
got around the card disadvantage drawback by some means (e.g. Rancor, which
pops back into your hand when the creature it enchants dies) or made the
creature enchantments *so* benificial that they were worth the risk of
playing anyway in decks built for them (e.g. Empyrial Armor (sp?) which
can be a +7/+7 or more enchantment under the right circumstances).

(Not that WotC always creates a winner nowadays. Far from it, they still
design a number of stupid creature enchantments. But then, they design a
number of stupid Magic cards in all the categories. But at least beneficial
creature enchantments aren't the slam dunk losers they once were.)

WotC did not need to change the rules for all current, past, and future
creature enchantments to fix this problem. And it's a good thing, too,
because who knows how unbalanced some of the cards might have become had
they done so. They simply kept designing until they came up with usable
cards. There's no reason to believe WW couldn't do the same with First
Strike.

Fred

Quite right. Unfortunately, it is only seen in Animalism. It's a
function that could certainly see more widespread use. One could
certainly make a case for Obfuscate, Obtenbration and Quietus cards that
have a similar effect.

I've been giving some thought to how to deal with the Silence of
Death/Wolf Claws combo that Joe C. brought up. At least with the Dawn
Op/Skin of Night/Weather Control combo someone has to block you...so
there's a way to avoid it, don't block unless you have your own Skin of
Night. With the SoD/WC combo, there's no prior requirement...meaning
that it can be used in any combat regardless of how it got initiated.

The first thought is maneuver to long range. However, Protean's
manuevers are free as Joe pointed out and decks based on combat
typically have more maneuvers than those that don't. If FS did beat
Dodge/S:CE and this combo became more common, I could see people using
maneuvers at least as much as S:CE leading pitch decks to be more
useful... *ponders* LSJ, how much would it take for me to bribe you
into making FS first? *grin*

Seriously, though. Outside of trying to go to long (and adding Animalism
and DotB would prevent that) the only recourse left is, as Joe
mentioned, damage prevention. I'm not certain that's necessarily a bad
thing.

Animalism, Auspex (with a successful block), Celerity, Chimerstry,
Fortitude, Protean, Quietus and Vicissitude all provide combat cards
that prevent damage, convert aggravated damage to normal or reduce hand
strike damage. Serpentis and Necromancy both have actions that allow
future conversion of agg to normal, although Death Pact is pretty damned
useless if you ask me. So...it's not like only Fortitude can deal with
this. By my reckoning the only clans that might have a problem stopping
this combo is Malkavian, Tremere (and their antitribu), Lasombra and
Giovanni...and to a slightly less extent, Setites. Overall, that's not
a bad spread of vampires that can handle the combo.

At this point, First Strike is almost useless and it appears that
changing it could have a fairly drastic efffect on the metagame. I'd be
curious to see what environment develops out of extensive playtesting of
this issue.

Perhaps my perception is colored from playing a lot of Magic, were FS

you get into situations were it saves your minion damage, possibly
torporizing (or in the case of an ally, fatal) damage because you've
torporized or (or in the case of an ally, killed) the other minion first.
In Magic, that often *is* the situation since in Magic the whole combat
system is geared to single-round results with wounds being healed at the
end of each turn. In Jyhad, particularly with the larger minions, you
often get combat were the result is one turn of the two minions wounding
each other and then parting company.

to use that Ivory Bow or not.

previous cards was all about.

with the anti-equipment stuff, they overcosted the whole design element

suddenly turn out to become unstopable when the players start rebuilding
all their decks. My way's much safer, especially considering that I
don't believe the situation is all that bad right now. I think you're
way overstating to suggest that VTES is not playable for newbies. It's
fine for newbies. Or at least, to the extent it isn't, this isn't the
problem.

Fred

>Sidenote: LSJ stated that Scorpion Sting models the "FS beats dodge"

Well, it doesn't MODEL it, but it certainly provides an effect similar
to it. You play a card to gain a dodge-proof strike, it's just that
it's not First Strike.

>You are mixing some things up here: we are talking about dodges and FS
>here, not FS and Potence-strikes.

OK, I think it's time to go back and restate the basic ideas..

Proposal: Should First Strike beat S:CE/Dodge?
Addition: If it does, should a CEL card granting First Strike in some
form be created to make the mechanic useful?

Therefore for the arguments below, we assume that First Strike *does*
beat S:CE/dodge, and there is such a CEL card.

The reason Potence strikes keep coming in is that in creating a new
card, you need to analyze its effect against ANY sort of deck, whether
it be combat-avoidance or combat-intensive. Potence provides IG, a
heavy combat trump in itself, but also fairly necessary since Potence
is somewhat card-intensive.

>Making FS beat S:CE is a Bad Thing, can't really state why, it just
>seems too powerful to me. FS beating dodge was always viewed as "making
>no difference" before. Now it seems as a too powerful concept, too. :)

FS beating S:CE I don't care for, for reasons above. FS beating dodge
seems sort of meaningless to me - it'd be amusing, but you'd probably
see a visible shift in the metagame towards S:CE and away from "dodge"
as a result - IF anyone played with the First Strike card instead of
additional strikes.

>How is the qui/pro approach (in regards to FS beating dodge) different
>than cel/pro? Right *now* you can only use damage prevention and S:CE
>against a dedicated cel/pro deck. No-one ever complained about that,
>though cel/pro is a lot more easier to pull off than qui/pro (even *if*
>FS beat dodge). The defenses against the qui/pro combo would also be
>S:CE and damage prevention.

Qui/Pro beats everything. You must prevent the damage, reduce their
hand damage, or die. AND, most importantly, you do not get to hit
back unless you prevent.

Cel/Pro falls over to S:CE (one big difference), and ALSO falls over
to being hit back, which is a HUGE difference. The classic
Brujah/Gangrel combat goes mostly with the Brujah playing TS/IG/Blur
and pounding the Gangrel for 9 points of damage while the Gangrel
whips out his Wolf Claws and pokes the Brujah's eye out. Then the
Gangrel plays Skin of Steel, the Brujah plays superior Sideslip, and
everyone goes away unhappy. If either person doesn't have their
prevent handy, they get clobbered. Cel/Pro doesn't have easy access
to Fortitude, so they don't even have the option to prevent - they
will always get clobbered. When combat will result in mutual
torporisation, it starts to be a judgement call on whether it's worth
it or not.

>cel/pro also requires only a 2-card combo: initial strike gets dodged by
>opponent, then play additional strike and Wolf Claws. 2 cards, not hard
>to pull off.
>Or: Acrobatics and then Wold Claws. Also 2 cards, better against damage
>dealing decks (pot, pro).
>The only difference I can see is that qui/pro with FS beating dodge
>wouldn't have to fear IG. Bad Thing? There is currently not much that
>can be done against IG, which is often viewed as a combat trump card.

You can always maneuver away from IG, or hit back. Qui/Pro would
currently trash IG decks anyway, just because First Strike is, well,
first. That's fine. But Qui/Pro needs a weakness, and that weakness
is, unfortunately, S:CE and Dodge. Otherwise, it would HAVE no
weakness and everyone would be forced to play with prevent cards of
some form. Much like what happened when weenie bleed became all the
rage - people were playing with weenies themselves OR playing with
10-12 Deflections. That was a bit of a problem, and still is,
although people are figuring out better ways to deal with weenies.
(And the prevalence of combat decks is making it a lot tougher for
them to live.)

>> > Well, superior Shadow Step surely beats the combo, as will
>> > do the help of Terror Frenzy.
>>

>> Good point. I forgot about those. Scratch Lasombra from the list.
>

>As well as the Tzimisce, Gangrel, !Gangrel, Nosferatu, !Nosferatu,
>Ravnos due to Terror Frenzy and Aid From Bats. (Easy combo).

The point isn't how many clans DON'T have access to a way around it...
it's that forcing people to play some form of prevent in their decks
is a Bad Thing(tm). Also, the Tzimisce/Gangrel/Nossies may have
access to Terror Frenzy/Aid from Bats, but it sort of goes against
their natural strategies, since VIC, PRO, and POT all are close-range
combat discplines.

>> Ayup. Of course, if there's no one left to stop you, it's that much
>> easier. But if you have a short (2-3 cards) combat combo that sends
>> vampires to torpor with little risk, bruise and bleed becomes even
>more
>> abusive than stealth and bleed.
>
>Bah, why should bruise and bleed be prohibited, whereas stealth and

>bleed is viewed as an integral part of the game? The *same* defences
>that work against s&b work against b&b. I don't view b&b as a very

>viable strategy. Not even if I could *almost* guarantee torporization of

>the blocker (which I can't). They simple don't try to block, and you get
>hand jam. Period.

Hm. A well-built S&B deck isn't vulnerable to the "i don't block you"
strategy, although it may get caught once or twice as a result. Just
the same, a well-built B&B deck isn't vulnerable to it either, since
when he has a handful of combat cards, those unblockable bleeds for 1
start to add up. And as soon as you're forced into combat somehow,
you KNOW he just picked up a handful of bleed cards.

I had a fairly functional PRE/POT bruise-bleed deck that I played for
awhile. The trick is to remember that it's "bruise and bleed", not
"kill and bleed". Don't torporise anything that moves, but just
merely whack the hell out of it every time you got blocked. It packed
20 Social Charms, 8 Rushes, and enough POT combat to do, on average, 5
points of damage to anything that blocked you (enough to kill a lot of
minions, actually.) I tended to play it by wasting some cards and
killing the first vampire to block me, which helped encourage people
not to block me. Then I bled until I ran out of bleed cards, and by
then I usually had a Rush in my hand. So I Rushed my predator to
cycle my combat hand, and then went back to bleeding. It worked
pretty well...

Shame the Tremere can't do something like this. =)

>But I think we have drifted quite far away from the initial topic: FS
>should beat dodge in the new rule-book which hopefully comes out soon.

In your opinion. I say that FS beating dodge is a worthless and
equally-confusing change (wait, so it beats this one thing but not
this other thing? huh?), since you can just play additional strikes.

Messages.Body:
lor...@yahoo.com (Derek Ray) wrote:
> Qui/Pro beats everything. You must prevent the damage, reduce their
> hand damage, or die.

...or convert the agg damage to normal. Which leads me to...

> Cel/Pro doesn't have easy access to Fortitude, so they don't even
> have the option to prevent - they will always get clobbered.

Not true. Flesh of Marble limits damage to 1 and Adaptability converts
agg to regular at minor and prevents at superior. Celerity has Sideslip
(as you mentioned earlier) which, at superior, also prevents the 1
damage. Cel/Pro doesn't need Fortitude cards.

> You can always maneuver away from IG, or hit back. Qui/Pro would
> currently trash IG decks anyway, just because First Strike is, well,
> first.

Well...right now, it's third. ;)

> That's fine. But Qui/Pro needs a weakness, and that weakness
> is, unfortunately, S:CE and Dodge. Otherwise, it would HAVE no
> weakness and everyone would be forced to play with prevent cards of
> some form.

Here lies the crux of the problem. S:CE is viewed as too powerful,
primarily because it's too easy and cheap to pull off, resulting in the
strong desire to develop something that trumps it.

The thing being discussed to trump it, FS beating S:CE and Dodge,
results in exactly two very specific instances that require damage
prevention to trump _those_ instances, which I've given some more
thought to.

The first of those instances is a _unique_ ally, Muddles, equipping a
_unquie_ weapon, Ivory Bow, or a Flamethrower, for a total of 3 or 6
pool, respectively. Anytime you hinge a strategy on a single vampire,
it only takes someone to disable the vampire to shut you down. It's
even more true of an unique ally with only one life counter. Needless
to say, I view this a very fragile combo to sustain.

The second, SoD/WC requires Pro/Qui which naturally occurs on only one
vampire which costs 6 pool. I have had a little more time to think this
one out and I realized that the mention of Protean and Quietus weenies
leaves out an important fact. You have to get the discipline cards on
them and you can only play one per turn under normal conditions. This
results in the very likely probability that the hand will get clogged
with about 3-4 master cards because you need a bunch in order to make
sure they're available in your opening hand.

The weenie Potence IG deck kicks out a bunch of little thugs that need
no further discipline cards. This means the Pro/Qui deck is more
vulnerable to Sudden Reversal and that it will take at _least_ two turns
to get a single usable vampire for the combo while the Potence weenie
deck can potentially produce three usable vampires on the first turn.

Bum's Rush gives a maneuver, which means that the opposing vampire must
have at least two maneuvers to get away...something that most non-pitch
decks don't have. Multiply that times a half dozen of the little
monsters coming at you on turn 3 or 4 and if any of them get you with an
IG, all S:CE and Dodge in the world isn't going to save you.

Keeping that in mind, you can modify the IG deck to use Dominate for
bleed or Presence for bleed or voting to make the VP count a little
higher. A SoD/WC deck can't be modified into a Bruise and Bleed
strategy because none of the participating clans can bleed worth a sh*t
without Computer Hacking.

So...even after all the hoopla, SoD/WC is still not as likely to rack up
the VP's which will quickly result in it becoming a vicious, yet rarely
used, combo.

>>>> Well, superior Shadow Step surely beats the combo, as will
>>>> do the help of Terror Frenzy.
>>>
>>> Good point. I forgot about those. Scratch Lasombra from the list.
>

> The point isn't how many clans DON'T have access to a way around it...
> it's that forcing people to play some form of prevent in their decks
> is a Bad Thing(tm).

Why? It's available in one form or another to almost all clans and
every vampire in the game can use Guardian Angel, Flak Jacket and
Leather Jacket. Damage prevention is widely available and I don't see
any problem with people adding some Damage Prevention in addition to
S:CE decks. The biggest problem is that S:CE has caused all non-IG
combat decks to be generally ineffective. If this forces people to
diversify their combat defense when building decks, I don't see the
problem.

> Shame the Tremere can't do something like this. =)

They can, it just requires Fortitude. Ironically the best For-Dom-Tha
dcampire for this is a Gangrel.

> In your opinion. I say that FS beating dodge is a worthless and
> equally-confusing change (wait, so it beats this one thing but not
> this other thing? huh?), since you can just play additional strikes.

This I agree with.

After all that, I'm not completely sold either way on the "First Strikes
First" debate but my leanings are still towards making First Strike
resolve before other strikes (incl. S:CE and Dodge) are declared.

calling a Dodge or Combat Ends a "strike" doesn't make sense,
semantically, but I understand it to be just a way of representing the
effect mechanically. I see First Strike the same way; it doesn't really
mean "Occurs before any other possible combat effect," it means "if two
guys are pounding each other, the guy with First Strike pounds first."

Well, agreed, exceptions are generally bad. But of course, every rule
in every game is an "exception", right from the one that tells you to open
the box and take out the playing pieces. First you establish general
procedures and principals. Then you tack on exceptions to the exceptions,
i.e., when there special cases. Then special cases to the special cases
and so forth. What emerges is the full set of rules. The question isn't
"are exceptions 'bad'" per se. Each piece of added complexity is always
'bad' if it has no reason to exist. But presumedly, they all have a reason
to exist that makes the game more fun in some sense, whether it's adding to
the scope of things that players can do or make the simulation (to the
extent the game is a simulation) seem more 'real' or possibly other purposes.

So your real point, I think, is to say that this exception doesn't add
to the fun of the game sufficiently to pull its weight in added complexity.
Which is fine as opinion. I might point out that either way, I think there's
going to be _some_ 'exception', since S:CE and Dodge say that you 'always'
ignore the other strike. So you'll be dropping the resolve-first-strike-
strikes-first exception in favor of one that says, "Dodge and S:CE don't
work in the case that the other strike has the first strike property".
Intuitively, there's probably a better argument for that. But it's still
just an argument and bottom line, these are still 'exceptions'.

>Now if that's not something that could be made easier, as I gather most
>people think it wouldn't have any impact on game-play. So why do we need the
>exception with dodge?
>There simply is no reason other "because it was designed that way" which
>I know LSJ would state. :)
>With keeping the goal of making the rules more streamlined (not
>simpler!) we should help newbies and alter dodge. :)

It absolutely has an effect on game play. It makes all the difference in the
world when designing Celerity decks, IMHO (amongst others; but I think of
Celerity decks first because they Dodge-with-an-additional-strike(s) all the
time, thus producing offense will remaining 'untouchable' on defence; with
this change, they would no longer be untouchable - HUGE difference!). And
'because it was designed that way' is a perfectly valid reason in view of
the fact that there's subjective judgment about how the combat system should
work. Essentially, the designers felt the game is more fun to play this way,
for whatever reasons.

Making rules streamlined is only one consideration. If it were the only
one in existence, there's no point to creating any games. The absolutely
*simplest* set of game rules (therefore the 'best' one by the measure of
simplicity alone) would be a null set - that is, the simplest game in
existence is to not play a game at all.

Fred

prea...@utanet.at wrote:
> Another issue is making all rules and mechanics more playable. What's
> the point of having a rule that has no use in the game, will some
> newbies ask (e.g. withdrawal, FS).

We've had the withdrawal rule come into play before.
Granted, it's not a frequent event by any stretch (esp. since we rarely
get to the end of our decks). All a player really have to know is
that the rule (whatever it is) exists. Then, if you get to the point in
the game where you think you might want to withdraw, you look up the
rule.

The best example of what the withdrawal rule is for was in one of our
games six months ago or so: two players left, and one with an empty
library (but plenty of equipment - mostly guns - in play).

The player with cards left had the advantage except for the guns, which
would've rapidly reduced the number of ready minions he had. So he needed
some time to build up strength for an assault. He was denied that time
by the other player's constant attempts to withdraw - which forced him to
send a minion over every turn to get shot up.

The withdrawal rules (and, to a greater extent, the Edge) seem to have been
created to ensure activity and prevent the game from stagnating (at the
end) as both players simply entrench and wait for the other player to stick
his neck out. This isn't quite as important in a tournament game with a
time limit, but has more application to the "regular" game.

Even if no one ever successfully withdraws (or if no one ever successfully
holds onto the Edge), the rule still serves a purpose.

Because of the logical steps involved.

* First, you alter FS to beat Dodge and S:CE.

. Now you already have a problem with Quietus/Protean being
overpowerful combat, although tricky to make work. BUT, this is
merely the tip of the iceberg. You also have a bigger problem with
the Muddled Vampire Hunter - see previous posts.

* Second, since you have gone to all the trouble to alter FS, you need
to make a card that uses FS so that it matters. So you make some
Celerity card that grants it. (It makes no sense to give it to
anything but Celerity.)

. Now you are REALLY creating a problem. Celerity is the premier
combat-support discipline, and ALREADY beats Dodge even without FS.
Potence/Celerity needs no help, but you've just given it some, making
it even more of a combat trump than it already was. You also have
given decks NO combat defense against someone who plays First Strike,
except to generate their OWN First Strike - meaning every deck should
have Celerity. Immortal Grapple can be beaten by just maneuvering
away from it - a properly built CEL/FS deck with such a card should
conceivably guaranteed-kill a vampire every combat, with no recourse
for the victims except something like Elysium or Fortitude (and
THA/CEL will even beat up Fortitude). Making POT/CEL do this with
Immortal Grapple is nowhere near as easy since you must include oodles
of maneuvers.

Making combat this powerful is not good. Combat decks attack
secondary resources, vampires. But without those secondary resources,
you can neither defend your own primary resources NOR remove someone
else's primary resources. A bleed or vote deck attacks your primary
resources, but while your primary resources are being depleted you
lose little to none of your ability to remove OTHERS' primary
resources, or defend against additional attacks. This is why it's
good for combat to be a "weak third" behind bleed and vote, the other
two archetypes - because making it equal is almost like making it
first. And that wouldn't be good at all.

>I don´t think it would unbalance the game, but as long as no one seems
>to actually "playtest" this it will remain a mysterium.

Nothing new is available to be playtested - therefore we are forced to
indulge in idle speculation and apply as much logic as we can to
things via the classic "what if?" =)

generally a good way to solve them.

>game? Following that kind of logic is not productive.

That was precisely my point. You can't simplyify to extreme or you
